The rain didn’t fall; it hung in the air, a grey curtain that smelled of iron and rot. Elias didn’t look up from his logbook. The ink was still wet, the date scrawled in jagged, frantic loops: *October 14, 1892*.

It was October 15.

A knock at the heavy oak door of the lighthouse keeper’s cottage shattered the silence. Elias didn’t move. He knew who it was. He had been expecting this for three days, ever since the brass telescope on the roof had begun to hum with a frequency that made his teeth ache.

The door creaked open. Wind whipped into the room, scattering the logbook.

"You’re late," Elias said, his voice rough from disuse. He finally looked up.

Standing in the doorway was a woman. She wore a coat of black rubber, slick with rain, and her face was obscured by a mask of glass and brass tubes. She stepped inside, the door slamming shut behind her with a boom that shook the dust from the rafters.
